notes:
I found notes for most verses, but there are gaps, and some limits you should know about first:

- **The Enduring Word page stopped loading before v. 12**, so I have nothing from it on vv. 25–48.
- **I didn't get to netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org**, so there are no modern-scholarship notes. The nearest is the older Expositor's Greek Testament (v. 46).
- **Nothing came up on Word of Faith or hyper-grace readings.** There's only one remark on prosperity preachers (v. 46).
- **Vv. 25, 32–34, 36, 39 and 47–48 have little or no coverage.**
- **No Lutheran-site sources.** The only Lutheran voice is Bengel, quoted on Bible Hub.
- **The StudyLight page used for vv. 45–47 came up in Spanish**, so those notes are my translation.

---

**v. 25** – Nothing found that comments on this verse by itself.

**v. 26**
- Barnes says these are the nobleman's own words, setting out how he will hand out rewards in his kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-27.html
- Benson says the single pound given to each servant seems to stand for the gospel, which is the same for everyone who hears it. The talents in Matthew 25, given in different amounts, stand for the different abilities God gives. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-27.htm

**v. 27** – *The traditional reading*
- Ellicott says only Luke has this detail. Its background is how Archelaus acted when he came back from Rome. Spiritually it shows Christ finally winning over the unbelieving and rebellious. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-27.htm
- Barnes, Gill and the Pulpit Commentary read it on two levels. Its first fulfilment is the destruction of Jerusalem. Behind that lies the final judgment of everyone who rejects Christ as King. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-27.htm
- Meyer says the strong word "slay" stands for complete condemnation at the final judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-27.htm

*Where traditions differ*
- **On the timing.** Constable says these enemies stand for unbelievers, judged after Christ returns. He notes that many amillennial and postmillennial interpreters instead see the fall of Jerusalem here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-27.html
- **Calvin (Reformed)** says the verse is aimed mainly at the Jews but covers everyone who rebels while the master is away. Its purpose was to warn rebels and also to keep Jesus' own people faithful. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-27.html

**v. 28**
- Ellicott says the wording shows the usual way they travelled: Jesus walking ahead and the disciples following. https://biblehub.com/luke/19-28.htm
- The Bible Hub notes say Jesus is not dragged to his fate but walks toward it willingly. https://biblehub.com/luke/19-28.htm
- Matthew Henry calls him the foremost of the company, as if eager to reach the place. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-29.html

**vv. 29–30**
- Constable links the Mount of Olives to the prophecy of the Messiah coming there (Zechariah 14:4). He says the colt fulfils Zechariah 9:9–10. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-29.html
- Barclay says the entry was carefully planned. It was an acted-out claim to be the Messiah, made with great courage while there was a price on Jesus' head. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-29.html
- Fortner (sovereign-grace Baptist) treats the story as an allegory as well as history. The tied colt pictures fallen people, and fetching it pictures God's irresistible saving grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-29.html

**v. 31** – Barclay thinks "The Lord needs it" was a password agreed long before. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-29.html

**vv. 32–34** – Got Questions points out that the owners were satisfied with that answer and let the disciples go. https://www.gotquestions.org/Palm-Sunday.html

**v. 35**
- Got Questions calls this the story of a King who came as a humble servant on a donkey. https://www.gotquestions.org/triumphal-entry.html
- Bridgeway says he came on a donkey as a king of peace, not on a horse as a conquering warlord. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-29.html

**vv. 37–38**
- John Piper (Desiring God) calls the day one of "great insight and great misunderstanding." The crowd was right that Jesus is the King. They were wrong to expect him to take the throne and free Israel from Rome. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/palm-sunday-tears-of-sovereign-mercy
- Orthodox: The OCA says Jesus let the people hail him publicly as king. The entry fulfils prophecies of the king who comes to set up a final kingdom. The people mistook it for the rise of a political messiah. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2026/04/05/20-entry-of-our-lord-into-jerusalem-palm-sunday
- The OCA also notes that worshippers carrying branches on Palm Sunday are judged together with the crowd. The same voices that cried Hosanna soon cried "Crucify him!" https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-church-year/lazarus-saturday-and-palm-sunday

**v. 39** – Bible Hub's study notes suggest the Pharisees also feared Rome's reaction, because publicly hailing a king could look like a political threat. https://biblehub.com/study/luke/19-40.htm

**v. 40** – *The traditional reading*
- Barnes says this is a proverb, not to be taken literally. The joy was right and shouldn't be held back. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-40.htm
- Ellicott hears an echo of Habakkuk 2:11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-40.htm
- Gill sees a hint that Gentiles, whom Jews compared to stones, would come to faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-40.htm
- The Expositor's Greek Testament mentions a minority view (Stier, Nösgen): the ruined stones of the temple would one day testify for Jesus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-40.htm

*Where readers differ*
- Bible Hub's own notes say Christ's words are literal. https://biblehub.com/luke/19-40.htm
- Matthew Henry, and the Catholic Haydock, both say it came true in effect at the crucifixion, when the rocks split. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-40.html
- **Wesley (Methodist):** God would raise up even more unlikely people to praise him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-40.html
- **Godbey (Holiness):** Jesus approved of loud worship, like a holiness camp meeting. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/msg/luke/19-40.html
- **Haydock (Catholic):** the proverb means nothing could stop God's decision to glorify Jesus that day. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-40.html

**v. 41** – *The traditional reading*
- Ellicott says this and Lazarus' grave are the only times Jesus' tears are recorded. https://biblehub.com/luke/19-41.htm
- The Cambridge Bible says Luke's word means weeping aloud, not silent tears. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-41.htm
- Constable says the fate of sinners who reject grace broke Jesus' heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-41.html

*Where traditions differ (God's will and those who refuse him)*
- **Calvin (Reformed):** Jesus wished his coming might bring salvation to all. He wept as Mediator, with his divinity "concealed." https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol32/htm/lxxxii.htm
- **Poole (Reformed):** rejects the view that Christ's tears mean God must give grace whether people obey or not. He says Christ wept as a man and as a minister of the gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-41.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** no one should hold "doctrines of truth" in a way that hardens them toward fellow sinners. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-41.htm
- **Bengel (Lutheran):** Jesus weeps yet forces no one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-41.htm
- **Coffman (Restoration Movement):** all of Jesus' efforts to prevent the disaster had been rejected. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-41.html

**v. 42**
- Calvin says the speech is broken off because of strong emotion. Grief is mixed with rebuke for refusing salvation. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol32/htm/lxxxii.htm
- A Bible Hub article links "hidden" to Isaiah 6:9–10: unbelief leads to God hardening people as judgment. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Jesus_cry_for_Jerusalem.htm

**v. 43**
- Calvin says Jesus now speaks as a judge, like the prophets who wept and still announced judgment. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol32/htm/lxxxii.htm
- Bengel notes that the Roman siege later began on that very spot. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-41.htm

**v. 44**
- A Bible Hub article says "visitation" means God himself had arrived in the flesh. It points to the destruction of AD 70 as fulfilment. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Jesus_cry_for_Jerusalem.htm
- Fortner says Jesus wept because the judgment came from despising "the time of their visitation." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-41.html

**v. 45**
- The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown commentary says John 2 records an earlier cleansing on Jesus' first visit; this second one came on his last. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-46.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary sees it as fulfilling Malachi 3:1–2. Rather than ending at a palace, the King's procession ends at the temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-45.html

**v. 46** – *The traditional reading*
- The quotations come from Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11 (Gill). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-46.htm
- Bible Hub's notes say a "den" is where criminals feel safe; the leaders used ritual as cover. https://biblehub.com/luke/19-46.htm
- Barclay says worship was being used to exploit worshippers, and Jesus acted out of passion for social justice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-46.html
- Ryle says the passage shows how much Christ dislikes the misuse of holy things. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/jmt/luke/19-46.html

*Older critical note*
- The Expositor's Greek Testament notes that Luke leaves out Isaiah's "for all nations." This may be to sharpen the contrast, or because the temple was already in ruins when Luke wrote. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-46.htm

*Catholic*
- Ambrose (in the Catena Aurea) reads it spiritually too. Dealers in the temple stand for people who make gain from Scripture, and the believer's soul is also a temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-45.html

*Prosperity teaching*
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) uses this verse to criticise faith preachers. He asks why men claiming great faith rely on mailing lists to keep their aircraft flying. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-45.html

**v. 47**
- Matthew Henry gives the verse ("he taught daily in the temple") but no comment of his appeared in the results. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-46.html
- The Catena Aurea says that when the soul learns to avoid evil, the truth teaches in that temple every day. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-45.html

**v. 48** – Nothing found.
